# sk-code-frontend: Manual Testing Playbook

Routing-recall corpus for the `sk-code-frontend` surface.

<!-- MANUAL_PLAYBOOK_RESULT_PERSISTENCE_CONTRACT -->
> **Result persistence**: a scenario run is complete only after its `PASS`, `FAIL` or `SKIP` outcome and
> reason are recorded into `sk-code/benchmark/reports/<dated-run-label>/`. The packet carries no
> `benchmark/` of its own, so its runs land in the hub's report tree.
>
> The record is written by hand, because the harness that once wrote it was retired with its lane.
> A manual run produces one dated folder holding a `README.md` with the verdict, the reason, the
> evidence paths and the scenario ids, and a `source.md` naming the spec packet that holds the raw
> transcript. The hub's own report index states that its rows are written by that harness at the
> moment it writes a report, so a hand-written run adds its folder and leaves that index alone; the
> folder name is what makes it findable.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

Two scenarios live here, one per intent family the surface routes: a web request that names `semantic html markup`, and a Figma check that names `figma frame check`. Each one sends a single exact prompt through the packet router, confirms the intent it selects, and confirms the resource set `RESOURCE_MAP` declares for that intent.

The intents and the map are read from the `MACHINE ROUTER` section at the end of [`ROUTER.md`](../ROUTER.md); the router's `INTENT MODEL` in section 2 and the reference map in [`SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md) carry the prose that names the same paths.

The hub's router-sync guard replays every scenario here that declares `expected_intent` (check `4` of `sk-code-skilled/assets/scripts/verify-router-sync.cjs`), and the guard walks packet-level playbooks only, so a routing scenario kept anywhere else would never be replayed. Every scenario in this corpus declares an intent, because every one of them makes a route claim.

### Categories

| # | Category | Folder | Scenario IDs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Frontend Surface | `frontend-surface/` | frontend-surface-web, frontend-surface-figma-check |

### Scenarios

| # | ID | Intent | File |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | frontend-surface-web | FRONTEND_WEB | [frontend-web.md](frontend-surface/frontend-web.md) |
| 2 | frontend-surface-figma-check | FIGMA_TO_CODE | [figma-check.md](frontend-surface/figma-check.md) |

A **routing** scenario, meaning one that declares `expected_intent` and `expected_resources`, is `PASS` when every path in its `expected_resources` resolves under the packet root, the replayed router selects that intent, and the router emits that path set for the exact prompt. It is `FAIL` when its checks do not hold, and `SKIP` only when a specific sandbox or runtime blocker prevented the run.

---

## 2. GLOBAL PRECONDITIONS

- Run every command from the repository root.
- The `sk-code` hub registers `sk-code-frontend` in `mode-registry.json`, so the packet is a known surface, and the compiled route serves the hub.
- Node is available for the router-sync guard and for the replay command each scenario runs.
- The packet is read-only and every scenario reads the same router and references, so a run writes nothing inside the repository and needs no fixture.

---

# sk-code-frontend: Manual Testing Playbook

Routing-recall corpus for the `sk-code-frontend` surface.

<!-- MANUAL_PLAYBOOK_RESULT_PERSISTENCE_CONTRACT -->
> **Result persistence**: a scenario run is complete only after its `PASS`, `FAIL` or `SKIP` outcome and
> reason are recorded into `sk-code/benchmark/reports/<dated-run-label>/`. The packet carries no
> `benchmark/` of its own, so its runs land in the hub's report tree.
>
> The record is written by hand, because the harness that once wrote it was retired with its lane.
> A manual run produces one dated folder holding a `README.md` with the verdict, the reason, the
> evidence paths and the scenario ids, and a `source.md` naming the spec packet that holds the raw
> transcript. The hub's own report index states that its rows are written by that harness at the
> moment it writes a report, so a hand-written run adds its folder and leaves that index alone; the
> folder name is what makes it findable.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

Two scenarios live here, one per intent family the surface routes: a web request that names `semantic html markup`, and a Figma check that names `figma frame check`. Each one sends a single exact prompt through the packet router, confirms the intent it selects, and confirms the resource set `RESOURCE_MAP` declares for that intent.

The intents and the map are read from the `MACHINE ROUTER` section at the end of [`ROUTER.md`](../ROUTER.md); the router's `INTENT MODEL` in section 2 and the reference map in [`SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md) carry the prose that names the same paths.

The hub's router-sync guard replays every scenario here that declares `expected_intent` (check `4` of `sk-code-skilled/assets/scripts/verify-router-sync.cjs`), and the guard walks packet-level playbooks only, so a routing scenario kept anywhere else would never be replayed. Every scenario in this corpus declares an intent, because every one of them makes a route claim.

### Categories

| # | Category | Folder | Scenario IDs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Frontend Surface | `frontend-surface/` | frontend-surface-web, frontend-surface-figma-check |

### Scenarios

| # | ID | Intent | File |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | frontend-surface-web | FRONTEND_WEB | [frontend-web.md](frontend-surface/frontend-web.md) |
| 2 | frontend-surface-figma-check | FIGMA_TO_CODE | [figma-check.md](frontend-surface/figma-check.md) |

A **routing** scenario, meaning one that declares `expected_intent` and `expected_resources`, is `PASS` when every path in its `expected_resources` resolves under the packet root, the replayed router selects that intent, and the router emits that path set for the exact prompt. It is `FAIL` when its checks do not hold, and `SKIP` only when a specific sandbox or runtime blocker prevented the run.

---

## 2. GLOBAL PRECONDITIONS

- Run every command from the repository root.
- The `sk-code` hub registers `sk-code-frontend` in `mode-registry.json`, so the packet is a known surface, and the compiled route serves the hub.
- Node is available for the router-sync guard and for the replay command each scenario runs.
- The packet is read-only and every scenario reads the same router and references, so a run writes nothing inside the repository and needs no fixture.

---

## 3. GLOBAL EVIDENCE REQUIREMENTS

13: # Web Cascade and Selectors
14: 
15: This file keeps the deeper cascade and selector mechanics. The baseline CSS architecture rules remain in [web-markup-and-css.md](web-markup-and-css.md).
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW AND CASCADE AND SPECIFICITY
20: 
21: ### CS1. Cascade decision order
22: 
23: **Rule.** Resolve competing declarations by origin and importance, layer order, specificity, scope proximity when scoped rules apply, then source order.
24: **Why.** The cascade compares these criteria in order, so a later rule cannot win by source order when an earlier criterion already decided the result.
25: **When not to.** Skip the comparison when the declarations do not apply to the same element and property.
26: **Pitfall.** Normal unlayered declarations outrank normal declarations in named layers, while important declarations reverse layer precedence.
27: **Support.** Judgment, no version gate.
28: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Cascade
29: 
30: ### CS2. Global cascade layer order
31: 
32: **Rule.** Declare the cascade layer order once in a global stylesheet before component styles load.
33: **Why.** Layer order is established the first time each layer name appears. Component style injection can vary with load order, so per-component layer blocks cannot define a reliable shared order.
34: **When not to.** Use unlayered styles only when the app deliberately relies on the unlayered precedence boundary.
35: **Pitfall.** A deeply scoped rule inside a layer loses to an unlayered rule even when its selector looks stronger.
36: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2024-09-14 (web-features `cascade-layers`). Chrome 99 / Firefox 97 / Safari 15.4.
37: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer
38: 
39: ### CS3. Specificity arithmetic with Angular emulation
40: 
41: **Rule.** Count IDs, class-like selectors and type selectors in separate specificity columns before changing a selector.
42: **Why.** IDs add to the first column, classes, attributes and pseudo-classes add to the second, and type selectors and pseudo-elements add to the third. A component-scoping attribute such as `[data-scope]` adds one class-like unit.
43: **When not to.** Do not raise specificity when the actual conflict comes from origin, importance or cascade layer order.
44: **Pitfall.** A selector such as `.card[data-scope]` has specificity `0-2-0`, not `0-1-0`.
45: **Support.** Judgment, no version gate.
46: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Specificity
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 2. SELECTOR LOGIC
51: 
52: ### CS4. Zero-specificity and maximum-argument selectors
53: 
54: **Rule.** Wrap low-priority defaults in `:where()` and use `:is()` when the matching alternatives should share the strongest argument's specificity.
55: **Why.** `:where()` contributes zero specificity, while `:is()` contributes the specificity of its most specific argument.
56: **When not to.** Keep a direct class selector when the alternatives would obscure which component states match.
57: **Pitfall.** Adding a high-specificity selector to one `:is()` alternative raises the specificity of the entire selector.
58: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2023-07-21 (web-features `is`). Chrome 88 / Firefox 82 / Safari 14.
59: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2023-07-21 (web-features `where`). Chrome 88 / Firefox 82 / Safari 14.
60: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/:is
61: 
62: ### CS5. Narrow relational matching with :has()
63: 
64: **Rule.** Keep `:has()` selectors narrow and close to the component that owns the matching relationship.
65: **Why.** The browser reevaluates relational matches as the relevant DOM changes, and a broad ancestor selector can increase style invalidation work.
66: **When not to.** Prefer an existing direct selector when the relationship is already represented by a simple parent or sibling structure.
67: **Pitfall.** A broad rule such as `body:has(.is-open)` makes unrelated subtree changes relevant to a page-level selector.
68: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2026-06-19 (web-features `has`). Chrome 105 / Firefox 121 / Safari 15.4.
69: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/:has
70: 
71: ---
72: 
73: ## 3. NESTING, SCOPE AND PROPERTIES
74: 
75: ### CS6. Native nesting and the nesting selector
76: 
77: **Rule.** Use `&` to make the parent selector explicit inside native CSS nesting.
78: **Why.** The nesting selector represents the full parent selector, so `&:hover` and `.theme &` express relationships without Sass-style string concatenation.
79: **When not to.** Keep a selector flat when nesting would hide its reach or increase selector complexity.
80: **Pitfall.** `&-active` does not append a suffix to a class name as it would in Sass.
81: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2026-06-11 (web-features `nesting`). Chrome 120 / Firefox 117 / Safari 17.2.
82: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_nesting/Using_CSS_nesting
83: 
84: ### CS7. Scoped selector boundaries
85: 
86: **Rule.** Use `@scope` to limit a rule to a component subtree when the required browsers support it.
87: **Why.** Scoped rules stop at the declared scope boundary, and scope proximity breaks a tie after specificity without changing the selector's specificity.
88: **When not to.** Use the established component scoping mechanism when a target browser does not support `@scope`.
89: **Pitfall.** A scope boundary does not prevent unscoped rules from matching the same descendants. In Safari 26.0 through 26.3, rules inside `@scope` do not apply to `<input>` and `<textarea>`; support is complete from 26.4.
90: **Support.** Baseline newly available since 2026-03-24 (web-features `scope`). Chrome 143 / Firefox 146 / Safari 26.4.
91: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@scope
92: 
93: ### CS8. Registered custom properties
94: 
95: **Rule.** Register a custom property with `@property` when its type, inheritance behavior or animation behavior must be explicit.
96: **Why.** Registration gives the browser a syntax, an `inherits` setting and an initial value, which lets typed values interpolate during animation.
97: **When not to.** Keep an unregistered property when it only carries an inherited token and needs no typed animation.
98: **Pitfall.** A registered property with the wrong `inherits` value can stop a theme token from reaching its descendants.
99: **Support.** Baseline newly available since 2024-07-09 (web-features `registered-custom-properties`). Chrome 85 / Firefox 128 / Safari 16.4.
100: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@property
101: 
102: ### CS9. Existing state selector contract
103: 
104: **Rule.** Follow the state selector contract in [web-markup-and-css.md Section 7](web-markup-and-css.md#7-css-architecture).
105: **Why.** The web layer already owns how exposed state reaches CSS selectors, so this file does not define a second state source. See [A5](web-accessibility-patterns.md#a5-focus-visible-styling) for the visible keyboard focus rule.
106: **When not to.** Use a class for a visual-only state that has no semantic state in the markup.
107: **Pitfall.** A store-owned `.is-open` class can drift from the expanded state already present on the control.

13: # Web Cascade and Selectors
14: 
15: This file keeps the deeper cascade and selector mechanics. The baseline CSS architecture rules remain in [web-markup-and-css.md](web-markup-and-css.md).
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW AND CASCADE AND SPECIFICITY
20: 
21: ### CS1. Cascade decision order
22: 
23: **Rule.** Resolve competing declarations by origin and importance, layer order, specificity, scope proximity when scoped rules apply, then source order.
24: **Why.** The cascade compares these criteria in order, so a later rule cannot win by source order when an earlier criterion already decided the result.
25: **When not to.** Skip the comparison when the declarations do not apply to the same element and property.
26: **Pitfall.** Normal unlayered declarations outrank normal declarations in named layers, while important declarations reverse layer precedence.
27: **Support.** Judgment, no version gate.
28: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Cascade
29: 
30: ### CS2. Global cascade layer order
31: 
32: **Rule.** Declare the cascade layer order once in a global stylesheet before component styles load.
33: **Why.** Layer order is established the first time each layer name appears. Component style injection can vary with load order, so per-component layer blocks cannot define a reliable shared order.
34: **When not to.** Use unlayered styles only when the app deliberately relies on the unlayered precedence boundary.
35: **Pitfall.** A deeply scoped rule inside a layer loses to an unlayered rule even when its selector looks stronger.
36: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2024-09-14 (web-features `cascade-layers`). Chrome 99 / Firefox 97 / Safari 15.4.
37: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer
38: 
39: ### CS3. Specificity arithmetic with Angular emulation
40: 
41: **Rule.** Count IDs, class-like selectors and type selectors in separate specificity columns before changing a selector.
42: **Why.** IDs add to the first column, classes, attributes and pseudo-classes add to the second, and type selectors and pseudo-elements add to the third. A component-scoping attribute such as `[data-scope]` adds one class-like unit.
43: **When not to.** Do not raise specificity when the actual conflict comes from origin, importance or cascade layer order.
44: **Pitfall.** A selector such as `.card[data-scope]` has specificity `0-2-0`, not `0-1-0`.
45: **Support.** Judgment, no version gate.
46: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Specificity
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 2. SELECTOR LOGIC
51: 
52: ### CS4. Zero-specificity and maximum-argument selectors
53: 
54: **Rule.** Wrap low-priority defaults in `:where()` and use `:is()` when the matching alternatives should share the strongest argument's specificity.
55: **Why.** `:where()` contributes zero specificity, while `:is()` contributes the specificity of its most specific argument.
56: **When not to.** Keep a direct class selector when the alternatives would obscure which component states match.
57: **Pitfall.** Adding a high-specificity selector to one `:is()` alternative raises the specificity of the entire selector.
58: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2023-07-21 (web-features `is`). Chrome 88 / Firefox 82 / Safari 14.
59: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2023-07-21 (web-features `where`). Chrome 88 / Firefox 82 / Safari 14.
60: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/:is
61: 
62: ### CS5. Narrow relational matching with :has()
63: 
64: **Rule.** Keep `:has()` selectors narrow and close to the component that owns the matching relationship.
65: **Why.** The browser reevaluates relational matches as the relevant DOM changes, and a broad ancestor selector can increase style invalidation work.
66: **When not to.** Prefer an existing direct selector when the relationship is already represented by a simple parent or sibling structure.
67: **Pitfall.** A broad rule such as `body:has(.is-open)` makes unrelated subtree changes relevant to a page-level selector.
68: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2026-06-19 (web-features `has`). Chrome 105 / Firefox 121 / Safari 15.4.
69: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/:has
70: 
71: ---
72: 
73: ## 3. NESTING, SCOPE AND PROPERTIES
74: 
75: ### CS6. Native nesting and the nesting selector
76: 
77: **Rule.** Use `&` to make the parent selector explicit inside native CSS nesting.
78: **Why.** The nesting selector represents the full parent selector, so `&:hover` and `.theme &` express relationships without Sass-style string concatenation.
79: **When not to.** Keep a selector flat when nesting would hide its reach or increase selector complexity.
80: **Pitfall.** `&-active` does not append a suffix to a class name as it would in Sass.
81: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2026-06-11 (web-features `nesting`). Chrome 120 / Firefox 117 / Safari 17.2.
82: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_nesting/Using_CSS_nesting
83: 
84: ### CS7. Scoped selector boundaries
85: 
86: **Rule.** Use `@scope` to limit a rule to a component subtree when the required browsers support it.
87: **Why.** Scoped rules stop at the declared scope boundary, and scope proximity breaks a tie after specificity without changing the selector's specificity.
88: **When not to.** Use the established component scoping mechanism when a target browser does not support `@scope`.
89: **Pitfall.** A scope boundary does not prevent unscoped rules from matching the same descendants. In Safari 26.0 through 26.3, rules inside `@scope` do not apply to `<input>` and `<textarea>`; support is complete from 26.4.
90: **Support.** Baseline newly available since 2026-03-24 (web-features `scope`). Chrome 143 / Firefox 146 / Safari 26.4.
91: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@scope
92: 
93: ### CS8. Registered custom properties
94: 
95: **Rule.** Register a custom property with `@property` when its type, inheritance behavior or animation behavior must be explicit.
96: **Why.** Registration gives the browser a syntax, an `inherits` setting and an initial value, which lets typed values interpolate during animation.
97: **When not to.** Keep an unregistered property when it only carries an inherited token and needs no typed animation.
98: **Pitfall.** A registered property with the wrong `inherits` value can stop a theme token from reaching its descendants.
99: **Support.** Baseline newly available since 2024-07-09 (web-features `registered-custom-properties`). Chrome 85 / Firefox 128 / Safari 16.4.
100: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@property
101: 
102: ### CS9. Existing state selector contract
103: 
104: **Rule.** Follow the state selector contract in [web-markup-and-css.md Section 7](web-markup-and-css.md#7-css-architecture).
105: **Why.** The web layer already owns how exposed state reaches CSS selectors, so this file does not define a second state source. See [A5](web-accessibility-patterns.md#a5-focus-visible-styling) for the visible keyboard focus rule.
106: **When not to.** Use a class for a visual-only state that has no semantic state in the markup.
107: **Pitfall.** A store-owned `.is-open` class can drift from the expanded state already present on the control.
108: **Support.** Judgment, no version gate.
109: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Attribute_selectors

13: # Web Cascade and Selectors
14: 
15: This file keeps the deeper cascade and selector mechanics. The baseline CSS architecture rules remain in [web-markup-and-css.md](web-markup-and-css.md).
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW AND CASCADE AND SPECIFICITY
20: 
21: ### CS1. Cascade decision order
22: 
23: **Rule.** Resolve competing declarations by origin and importance, layer order, specificity, scope proximity when scoped rules apply, then source order.
24: **Why.** The cascade compares these criteria in order, so a later rule cannot win by source order when an earlier criterion already decided the result.
25: **When not to.** Skip the comparison when the declarations do not apply to the same element and property.
26: **Pitfall.** Normal unlayered declarations outrank normal declarations in named layers, while important declarations reverse layer precedence.
27: **Support.** Judgment, no version gate.
28: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Cascade
29: 
30: ### CS2. Global cascade layer order
31: 
32: **Rule.** Declare the cascade layer order once in a global stylesheet before component styles load.
33: **Why.** Layer order is established the first time each layer name appears. Component style injection can vary with load order, so per-component layer blocks cannot define a reliable shared order.
34: **When not to.** Use unlayered styles only when the app deliberately relies on the unlayered precedence boundary.
35: **Pitfall.** A deeply scoped rule inside a layer loses to an unlayered rule even when its selector looks stronger.
36: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2024-09-14 (web-features `cascade-layers`). Chrome 99 / Firefox 97 / Safari 15.4.
37: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer
38: 
39: ### CS3. Specificity arithmetic with Angular emulation
40: 
41: **Rule.** Count IDs, class-like selectors and type selectors in separate specificity columns before changing a selector.
42: **Why.** IDs add to the first column, classes, attributes and pseudo-classes add to the second, and type selectors and pseudo-elements add to the third. A component-scoping attribute such as `[data-scope]` adds one class-like unit.
43: **When not to.** Do not raise specificity when the actual conflict comes from origin, importance or cascade layer order.

55: **Why.** `:where()` contributes zero specificity, while `:is()` contributes the specificity of its most specific argument.

64: **Rule.** Keep `:has()` selectors narrow and close to the component that owns the matching relationship.

77: **Rule.** Use `&` to make the parent selector explicit inside native CSS nesting.
78: **Why.** The nesting selector represents the full parent selector, so `&:hover` and `.theme &` express relationships without Sass-style string concatenation.

19: ## 1. OVERVIEW AND CASCADE AND SPECIFICITY
20: 
21: ### CS1. Cascade decision order
22: 
23: **Rule.** Resolve competing declarations by origin and importance, layer order, specificity, scope proximity when scoped rules apply, then source order.
24: **Why.** The cascade compares these criteria in order, so a later rule cannot win by source order when an earlier criterion already decided the result.
25: **When not to.** Skip the comparison when the declarations do not apply to the same element and property.
26: **Pitfall.** Normal unlayered declarations outrank normal declarations in named layers, while important declarations reverse layer precedence.
27: **Support.** Judgment, no version gate.
28: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Cascade
29: 
30: ### CS2. Global cascade layer order
31: 
32: **Rule.** Declare the cascade layer order once in a global stylesheet before component styles load.
33: **Why.** Layer order is established the first time each layer name appears. Component style injection can vary with load order, so per-component layer blocks cannot define a reliable shared order.
34: **When not to.** Use unlayered styles only when the app deliberately relies on the unlayered precedence boundary.
35: **Pitfall.** A deeply scoped rule inside a layer loses to an unlayered rule even when its selector looks stronger.
36: **Support.** Baseline widely available since 2024-09-14 (web-features `cascade-layers`). Chrome 99 / Firefox 97 / Safari 15.4.
37: **See also.** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer

39: ### CS3. Specificity arithmetic with Angular emulation
40: 
41: **Rule.** Count IDs, class-like selectors and type selectors in separate specificity columns before changing a selector.
42: **Why.** IDs add to the first column, classes, attributes and pseudo-classes add to the second, and type selectors and pseudo-elements add to the third. A component-scoping attribute such as `[data-scope]` adds one class-like unit.

45: **Support.** Judgment, no version gate.

# CI Surface: GitHub Actions Workflow Evidence

**Domain evidence** for the repository's GitHub Actions workflows under `.github/workflows/`.

The packet records four things:

- Each workflow rule, with the file and line that prove it.
- The workflows that must never be weakened.
- The one trigger that looks like drift and is not.
- Two scaffold templates.

It writes nothing. Read-only means this packet writes nothing, and it does not limit what the acting agent may do.

The workflow mode the hub pairs it with reads the evidence and applies it. When the hub routes this packet alone because no workflow mode scored, the acting agent reads and applies it directly.

A workflow change looks small and has a wide effect. One path filter decides which workflows a commit starts, one missing twin entry fails the gate that guards the source tree, and one switched-off workflow can remove the only check a branch ruleset requires. This packet keeps those facts in one place so a reviewer or author does not rebuild them from the workflow files and review history.

## 1. WHEN THE HUB BUNDLES THIS

- The task adds, edits or reviews a file under `.github/workflows/`, `.github/actions/` or `.github/scripts/`.
- A request names a GitHub Actions workflow, a path filter, a job timeout, a concurrency group, a permissions block or a required status check.
- A request asks whether a workflow trigger is intentional or drift.
- A request asks for the shape of a new workflow or job before it is written.
- The task edits, reviews or scaffolds a workflow, so the acting mode needs the rules and the protected set rather than a guess.

Formal findings-first review stays with `sk-code-review` and author-side quality gates stay with `sk-code-quality`. This surface supplies the workflow evidence both apply.

---

## 2. REFERENCE MAP

Rule data (`references/`):
- `references/ci-workflow-standards.md`: the rule index. Path parity, SHA-pinned actions, a README row per workflow, `set -euo pipefail`, fork and secret safety, matrix and `fail-fast`. Each row says whether a machine gate enforces it.
- `references/trigger-and-filter-rules.md`: the twin rule, the rebuild-commit skip rule, push-only scope for generated-path filters and the intentional exceptions table.
- `references/job-shape-rules.md`: timeouts, least-privilege permissions, the concurrency template, the composite setup action and the switch `if:` shape.
- `references/protected-set.md`: the repository CI profile and its keys, the workflows protected by function and the rules that follow from it.

Scaffold templates (`assets/`):
- `assets/workflow-template.yml`: a whole-workflow starting point.
- `assets/job-block-template.yml`: a single job starting point.
- `assets/ci-profile.template.json`: the profile a repository fills in so `/doctor:ci` reads its own switch names, branches, protected workflows and README instead of this repository's.

Workflow doctrine: the implement, debug and verify phases are the shared doctrine symlinked in as `references/workflow-implement.md`, `references/workflow-debug.md` and `references/workflow-verify.md`. The acting agent applies it.

---

## 3. SMART ROUTING

The hub bundles this surface when a CI-workflow signal fires; §1 WHEN THE HUB BUNDLES THIS lists every signal. The first leaf it loads is `references/ci-workflow-standards.md`, the rule index the other three references extend.

The parent hub `RESOURCE_MAP` carries the same four paths under `CI_WORKFLOW`, re-prefixed with `sk-code-ci/`, and the router-sync guard (`sk-code-skilled/assets/scripts/verify-router-sync.cjs`, leg 2) checks that the two lists stay equal.

Read [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) before selecting skill-local resources; open only the matched files.

---

## 4. SURFACE STANDARDS (the non-negotiables)

The rules below hold for every workflow change, whoever applies it.

### ✅ ALWAYS

- **ALWAYS** cite the workflow file and line behind a rule, and re-read that line before relying on it, because the workflow files change faster than this packet.
- **ALWAYS** read `references/protected-set.md` before any change to a workflow, a ruleset context or a repository variable that gates one.
- **ALWAYS** read the intentional exceptions table in `references/trigger-and-filter-rules.md` before flagging a trigger as drift.
- **ALWAYS** keep generated-path filters push-only, because a `pull_request:` filter that ignores a path can leave a required check pending.
- **ALWAYS** name a rule with no machine enforcement as honour-system, so a reader knows nothing will catch a lapse.

### ⛔ NEVER

- **NEVER** write, edit or scaffold a workflow from this packet. The tool surface is `Read`, `Bash`, `Grep` and `Glob`, and the acting mode, `/doctor:ci scaffold` or `/doctor:ci toggle` applies any change.
- **NEVER** switch off or weaken a protected workflow without a second named confirmation that restates its role.
- **NEVER** switch off `message-contract.yml` while its ruleset context is required.
- **NEVER** treat the message-contract every-branch push trigger as drift. It is a recorded exception.
- **NEVER** copy a live secret, token or repository variable value into a template or a reference.

### ⚠️ ESCALATE IF

- A request needs a workflow file edited, because that is the acting mode's work and not this packet's.
- A cited line no longer matches the quoted text, so the rule data is stale and needs a refresh before it is trusted.
